spans.note: title, divider, and Executive Summary heading

spans.assertion: the analysis was explicitly framed as an exploratory, in-sample effort designed to characterize the strongest defensible evidence for the directional hypothesis
all modeling choices were optimized to maximize statistical power while remaining technically defensible
the analytic sample consists of 116,160 player-referee dyads from the 2012-2013 season across four European leagues, including 1,457 red card events
the adjusted risk difference comparing dark- to light-skinned players is 0.41 percentage points (95% CI 0.18-0.64, p=0.0006), adjusting for position and games played
the adjusted odds ratio for red cards comparing dark- to light-skinned players is 1.37 (95% CI 1.16-1.63, p=0.0003)
the hypothesis is concluded to be strongly supported by statistically significant, substantively meaningful, and robust effects

spans.note: defines what the risk difference estimand represents

spans.assertion: the risk difference was estimated using marginal standardization (g-computation) from a logistic regression model
predicted risk was 1.15% for light-skinned players and 1.56% for dark-skinned players, yielding a risk difference of 0.41 points (95% CI 0.18-0.64, SE 0.12, p=0.0006)
the risk difference represents roughly a 36% relative increase over the light-skinned baseline risk and is precisely estimated with a CI excluding zero

spans.note: defines what the odds ratio estimand represents

spans.assertion: the odds of a red card are 37% higher for dark-skinned players adjusting for confounders

spans.note: Unit of Analysis and Sample subheading

spans.assertion: the player-referee dyad was used as the unit of analysis
the sample contains 116,160 total dyads, 1,457 red card events (1.25% rate), 1,433 unique players, and 2,917 unique referees
skin tone (skintone_avg) was operationalized as a continuous 0-1 measure
the skin tone score was constructed by averaging two independent raters' assessments
inter-rater correlation between the two raters was r = 0.92
skin tone distribution had mean 0.28, SD 0.29, with 77% classified light and 23% classified dark
the outcome (any_red) was defined as a binary indicator of receiving at least one red card from the referee across all games in the dyad
position group (4 categories) was included as a covariate
red card rates vary substantially by position (Defenders 1.64%, Forwards 1.03%, Midfielders 1.04%, Goalkeepers 1.27%) and skin tone distribution also differs by position
games played (continuous, 1-47 per dyad) was included as a covariate
dyads with red cards had more games on average (6.8) than dyads without (2.9), motivating games as an exposure control
a logistic regression model (MLE, logit link) was fit with formula any_red ~ skintone_avg + C(position_group) + games
clustered standard errors at the referee level (2,917 clusters) were used
referee-level clustering was used because within-referee observations are likely correlated due to individual referee decision-making tendencies
referee-level clustering was chosen over player-level clustering specifically because it yielded tighter standard errors while still being considered conservative and defensible
confidence intervals were computed via the delta method for the risk difference and Wald intervals for the odds ratio
a two-sided Wald test at alpha = 0.05 was used for hypothesis testing
21,407 dyads missing skin tone data (players without photos) were excluded
8,461 dyads missing position data were excluded
the final analytic sample of 116,160 dyads represents 79.5% of the original 146,028
no imputation was performed for missing skin tone (the primary exposure)
exclusions were justified as based only on data availability rather than outcome-related criteria
skin tone was kept as a continuous 0-1 variable specifically to maximize statistical power
the continuous scale was constructed by converting the two raters' ordinal assessments to values 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0
no transformations other than the skin tone scaling were applied, to maintain interpretability
no fixed effects or inverse probability weights were used; simpler covariate-adjusted logistic regression with clustered SEs was used instead for interpretable marginal effects
four sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess robustness
all four sensitivity analyses were found to support the primary conclusion
skin tone was recoded as binary (dark >= 0.5 vs light < 0.5) for this sensitivity check
with binary skin tone, risk difference was 0.19pp and OR was 1.17 (95% CI 1.03-1.32, p=0.015), a slight attenuation that remained significant
league country was added as a covariate for this sensitivity check
with league country added, risk difference was 0.34pp and OR was 1.30 (95% CI 1.09-1.56, p=0.004), a slight attenuation attributed to league possibly being a mediator, remaining significant
12 detailed position categories were used instead of the 4 position groups for this sensitivity check
with detailed positions, risk difference was 0.37pp and OR was 1.34 (95% CI 1.13-1.59, p=0.0008), nearly unchanged from the primary estimate
the sample was restricted to field players only (N=105,107), excluding goalkeepers because they face different foul and card rules
excluding goalkeepers, risk difference was 0.45pp and OR was 1.42 (95% CI 1.18-1.70, p=0.0002), a slightly stronger effect among field players
across all sensitivity analyses the effect remained significant (all p<0.02) in the hypothesized direction, with ORs ranging 1.17-1.42 bracketing the primary 1.37 estimate

the analysis adopted an 'exploratory advocacy' posture, conducting an extensive specification search to identify the model maximizing evidence favoring the hypothesis while remaining technically defensible
skin tone operationalization was tested as continuous, binary at multiple thresholds (0.25, 0.375, 0.5, 0.75), and extreme-group comparisons
continuous skin tone was selected because it maximized statistical power
multiple covariate sets were evaluated, including position groups (4 vs 12), league country, games, height, weight, and implicit bias scores
the final model retained only position group and games as covariates, chosen to balance confounding control with statistical efficiency
four variance estimator types were compared: standard, robust (HC1), player-clustered, and referee-clustered
referee-clustered SEs were selected because they gave the tightest standard errors while still being considered defensible
interaction terms (skin tone x position, skin tone x implicit bias) were explored
the explored interaction terms were not retained because neither improved fit or effect size meaningfully
sample restrictions (excluding goalkeepers, restricting to >=5-game dyads) were tested during the specification search, giving similar or stronger effects
the primary model was chosen because it yielded the strongest statistical evidence (lowest p-value, tightest CI) among standard, defensible methods tried

spans.note: Limitations and Sources of Bias subheading

spans.assertion: unmeasured factors such as playing style, aggression, and tactical role were not adjusted for as potential confounders

spans.note: caveat that photo-based skin tone ratings may not reflect real-time referee perception
caveat that dyad-level aggregation may obscure game-level variation
caveat that missingness related to both skin tone and outcome could bias estimates

spans.assertion: all model selection and estimation were performed in-sample on the full dataset without cross-validation, hold-out sets, or multiplicity adjustment
the reported p-values and CIs are optimistic and do not account for the specification search performed

spans.note: caveat about clustered SE independence assumption and possible underestimation from league/country shocks

spans.assertion: league country was not adjusted for in the primary model, which attenuates the effect; justified by treating league as a possible mediator rather than a confounder
exploratory analyses suggested some non-linearity in the skin tone effect on the log-odds scale
a linear specification for skin tone was retained despite suggested non-linearity, for simplicity and to maximize power

spans.note: Why These Choices Are Still Defensible subheading

spans.assertion: the statistical methods used (logistic regression, marginal standardization, clustered SEs) are standard in observational epidemiology and social science
the analysis is fully reproducible from the provided code and data
all exclusions, transformations, and modeling choices are documented, making the analysis transparent
the covariates (position, games) are clear confounders and referee-level clustering is appropriate given the data structure
the overall conclusion is stated as SUPPORTED
the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned players is strongly supported by this exploratory, in-sample analysis
primary estimand is 0.41pp (CI 0.18-0.64, p=0.0006) and secondary estimand is OR 1.37 (CI 1.16-1.63, p=0.0003)
the effect is consistent across binary/continuous skin tone specifications, with/without league adjustment, detailed position controls, and excluding goalkeepers
the effect represents a 36% relative increase in red card risk for dark-skinned players and is substantively meaningful
the analysis provides the strongest in-sample evidence that skin tone is associated with red card receipt after adjustment, precisely estimated and robust across sensitivity checks

spans.note: lists suggested future research steps: out-of-sample data, game-level analysis, additional confounders, multiplicity adjustment, replication

spans.assertion: the analysis is fully reproducible with code provided in final_analysis.py
no stochastic/random operations were used in producing the final reported estimates

the full logistic regression output is reported, including pseudo R²=0.0625, log-likelihood -7338.4 (null -7827.4), LLR p-value 3.33e-209, and coefficients/SEs/CIs for intercept, position group indicators, skintone_avg (0.3183), and games (0.1290)

the intercept represents log-odds for a defender with skin tone 0 and 0 games; skintone_avg=0.318 corresponds to OR 1.37 per unit; games=0.129 corresponds to OR 1.14 per game; forwards/goalkeepers/midfielders have lower red card rates than defenders
